1:
What period the prophet is describing when he says Israel has been without the true God is the chapter's one real crux, and the commentary divides five ways on it. Henry sets out three readings without choosing between them: that it looks back as far as the days of the Judges, when they had priests but no teaching priests and elders but no law to any purpose; that it describes the ten tribes in Asa's own day, since Jeroboam's pretence of honouring the God who brought them out of Egypt had ended in downright infidelity, and no wonder when Jeroboam's priests were not teachers, for it is next to impossible that any religion should be kept up without a preaching ministry; or that the whole passage should be read in the future tense. Clarke reports the same diversity and does choose, judging the reference to the people under Rehoboam and Abijah, happily changed under Asa, the most natural sense, against those who make it a prophecy of the final destruction of the Jews as a political existence. Ellicott takes it as past and illustrative, periods of religious decline such as those recorded in the Book of Judges as well as later ones, adduced as historical proof that the Lord was with Israel while they were with him. Gill canvasses the Targum for the days of Jeroboam, the future reading fulfilled in the Babylonish captivity, and a Jewish reading by which the prophet foretold days when judgment should not be done in the world and the high priesthood and the sanhedrim should cease.

Delitzsch refuses all three tenses and argues the grammar instead. The words must be taken in a general sense with neither a preterite nor a future supplied but the first clause put in the present, so that many days are for Israel without the true God and without teaching priests and without law; and he holds that many days is not an accusative of time, against the editor he is answering, but the subject of the sentence, the preposition expressing not being in a condition but coming into it. He then allows the historical range the others quarrel over: Israel had already experienced such days in the defection after Joshua, but would experience them more often and more enduringly under the idolatrous kings, in the Assyrian and Babylonian exile, and still even now in its dispersion among all nations, which he supports from the threat Hosea utters with manifest reference to this verse.

On the conditional promise that frames the speech Clarke turns polemical. That the Lord is with you while you are with him is the settled and eternal purpose of God, and in this verse, he says, the unconditional perseverance of the saints has no place, being a doctrine which was first the ruin of the human race in the words ye shall not die and has ever since been the plague and disgrace of the Church. Henry reads the same clause as both comfort and caution, that those who keep close to God shall always have his presence but no longer than they keep close. Ellicott notes that the promise generalises the statement before it and is a favourite formula with the chronicler, and would render the verbs as present rather than future, he is found and he forsaketh. Clarke also quotes the Targum, which he calls curious, for its paraphrase that the Word of the Lord shall be your helper while you walk in his ways, and that if you cast away his fear he will abandon you. On the closing exhortation Ellicott supplies the moral: the ruinous results of not seeking Jehovah have been briefly but powerfully sketched from the nation's past history, and the conclusion is that they are not to fall away like their forefathers, the work for which there is a reward being the rooting out of idolatry.
8:
The name of the prophet in verse eight is corrupt, and the two who notice it differ on the repair. Ellicott is most thorough: the Hebrew gives the prophecy and then Oded the prophet without any connection, which is suspicious and suggests a marginal gloss that has crept into the text, especially since the opening verse names not Oded but Azariah son of Oded as the author. He proposes instead a gap in the text, the original running that this was the prophecy which Azariah son of Oded the prophet spake, and notes that the Hebrew manuscripts show no variation while the versions only prove the difficulty ancient. Gill concludes without the apparatus, mentioning the suggestion that a prophecy of the father was also delivered though not recorded, but preferring to identify Oded here with the son of Oded, as the Vulgate and Syriac and one Greek copy already do.

On what Asa then did the disagreement is narrower but real. Ellicott takes the renewal of the altar as reconsecration, the context implying it had been defiled by an illegal worship and the Greek and Latin both rendering it dedicated, while allowing the word may only mean repaired; he notes the altar had now stood sixty years. Clarke suggests instead that Asa enlarged it, so that more sacrifices might be offered than before, since it cannot be supposed an altar had no victims on it until the fifteenth year of a king already zealous for restoring worship. Henry reads the detail devotionally: the altar had gone out of repair though it was not above thirty-five years since Solomon's head was laid, so soon do ceremonial institutions wax old as things which in the fulness of time must vanish away. Ellicott also handles the cities taken from the hill country of Ephraim, where the reference is generally thought inaccurate and to belong to Abijah's conquests, since Asa had as yet no war with the north, though he allows Asa may have annexed border towns without resistance after his victory.

The incomers and the oath are read with one mind. Ellicott identifies the strangers as members of the northern kingdom and compares the accessions under Rehoboam and Hezekiah, and works at the puzzle of Simeon, whose territory lay inside Judah's inheritance, suggesting either that part of the tribe had migrated northward and some now settled back, or that Simeon was religiously isolated by the illegal worship at Beersheba, though this hardly agrees with the clause that they fell to him out of Israel. Clarke gives their motive, that men who had reflected on the promise to the house of David and found Jeroboam's government founded in idolatry would naturally leave their own country through a spirit of piety, to go where they might worship the true God. Henry notices the reciprocity, that they came because they saw the Lord was with Asa and that his notice of them encouraged them in turn, and that although he ordered their gathering the text says they gathered themselves, making it their own act. Clarke sets out the covenant in two parts, to seek the God of their fathers with all the heart and to put to death any who would not, so that no toleration was given to idolatry; and Gill adds from Piscator that they passed between the pieces of a calf cut asunder. Ellicott supplies the calendar and the legal frame: the appointed day fell in the third month, Sivan, answering to part of May and June; entering into the covenant means binding themselves by an oath, whose death clause is a sanction prescribed by the law of Deuteronomy; and the phrase rendered with their whole desire means with perfect willingness. On the result he renders the clause not that God was found of them but that he was at hand to them, in accordance with Azariah's promise at the outset.
16:
The deposing of the queen-mother is read as courage, as precedent, and as philology. Henry calls it bravely done of Asa that he would not connive at idolatry in those nearest him; he knew he must honour God more than his grandmother, and dared not leave an idol in an apartment of his palace while destroying idols in the cities of his kingdom. He supposes she may have subscribed the association and so escaped the death the covenant decreed, though Asa still stripped her of her dignity and probably confined her to privacy lest she infect others. Ellicott establishes that mother means grandmother and dismisses the theory that the mother of Abijah and the so-called mother of Asa were different women, one a daughter of Absalom and the other of Uriel of Gibeah: there are really no grounds for it, and she held the rank through her son's short reign and her grandson's too, until deposed for her idolatry. Clarke reports the Jewish tradition that she repented and her name was changed to Michaiah daughter of Uriel, so that no mention of the former name should reproach her.

On the idol itself Ellicott does the close work. The word rendered idol means a thing of fear, a horror, found only here and in the parallel; the phrase translated in a grove should rather be for Asherah; and the stamping, which he would render crushing, is the chronicler's own detail, as with Moses and the golden calf. On the unremoved high places Ellicott prefers a fresh explanation of the discrepancy with the earlier chapter: that passage relates what the good king resolved and attempted, while this one records his want of success, owing to the obstinate attachment of his people to their old sanctuaries, and he applies the same solution to a later contradiction. Clarke divides it differently, holding that Asa totally suppressed the idolatry but permitted some of the places or altars to remain. Henry offers a third account, that those in Judah's cities went but not those in the recovered cities of Israel, or that those for false gods went but not those used in the service of the God of Israel; and the moral he draws is that there may be defects in particular duties where the heart is still upright, since sincerity is something less than sinless perfection.

The closing date is the chapter's other textual difficulty, and it produces three incompatible repairs. Ellicott observes that the chronicler has evidently modified the older text, which says war continued between Asa and Baasha all their days, in order to date the outbreak of hostilities precisely, and that the verse of Kings need not imply more than that no amicable relations were ever established between two sovereigns who had inherited a state of war. He relays the solution of Thenius, that a letter standing for thirty entered the text when a transcriber wrote twice over the letter beginning the next word, so that the original readings were the fifth and sixth years and Baasha's attempt preceded the invasion; the false dates, he adds, probably existed already in the chronicler's own source. Clarke reports Ussher's view that the reckoning runs from the separation of the kingdoms and so falls in Asa's fifteenth year, suggests we should probably read the five and twentieth, and then enters the chapter's most candid remark: to settle these chronologies is a most difficult undertaking, and the difficulty does not belong to the sacred books alone, since all other chronological tables of all the nations of the world are in the same predicament, having often been puzzled by those of his own country even with access to all its archives. Gill limits the claim instead, taking it to mean only that there was no further war with a foreign enemy, since animosities and hostilities of some sort continued with Baasha as long as he lived.
